records.summary: 1326 Grant Ave has operated as a bar since at least 1999 with an active Type 48 (full-liquor bar) license issued January 2024. The property sits in the North Beach NCD where bars are a conditional use on the first story, and the North Beach Special Use District permits intensification of an existing bar without a new Conditional Use Authorization if the space is not enlarged. The site history shows continuous bar use with multiple ownership changes approved as continuations (2006, 2010, 2023). The immediate block is heavily saturated: 56 food/drink businesses within 500 feet, 13 of them bars, and 45 active on-sale ABC licenses within 500 feet (107 within 1,000 feet)—triggering an undue-concentration flag. Nearby precedent is limited but favorable: a 2012 CUA at 1337–39 Grant approved amplified live entertainment with extended hours to 1:30 a.m., and a 1994 CUA at the same block approved live entertainment in a café, though the base-rate count is too low (N=7 use decisions in 10 years) to show an approval rate.

patterns.pattern: Adding live entertainment or amplified entertainment to existing bars and restaurants in the North Beach NCD has consistently been approved via Conditional Use Authorization on the Grant Avenue corridor over three decades (1993–2012).

Amendments to existing CUAs to intensify entertainment (add amplification, extend hours past midnight to 1:30 a.m.) have been approved in North Beach NCD when the underlying use remains the same and no physical expansion occurs.

The subject property at 1326 Grant Ave has a documented entertainment approval history: a 2001 agency referral approved non-amplified live entertainment under a 1994 CUA (Motion 13769), establishing precedent for entertainment at this address.

Place of Entertainment and entertainment intensification applications that bypass the conditional use process and attempt approval via miscellaneous permit alone have been denied or flagged as requiring Commission review.

Hour extensions and changes of hours for bars with entertainment have been approved via agency referral when consistent with prior CUA conditions, though these referrals carry less precedential weight than Commission decisions.

Bars that seek physical expansion (enlargement of space) in the North Beach NCD require a new CUA even when the use remains bar; one such application on this block was withdrawn, suggesting expansion is more scrutinized than intensification without enlargement.

findings.text: An active ABC Type 48 (on-sale general, public premises) license was issued at 1326 Grant Ave on January 17, 2024, and the rules read the space as a bar from that license type.
Planning approved bar use continuations at this address in 2006, 2010, and 2023, and approved non-amplified live entertainment under a 1994 CUA (Motion 13769) that was still in effect in 2001.

Planning Code § 780.3(c)(1)(A) permits intensification of an existing bar in the North Beach Special Use District only if the space is not enlarged; the description states intensification without tenant improvements, which if confirmed would avoid the new-use prohibition but not the CUA requirement for intensifying a conditional use.

A 2012 CUA at 1337–39 Grant Ave (44 meters away) approved amplified live entertainment and extended hours to 1:30 a.m., and a 1993 CUA at 1363–71 Grant Ave (64 meters) approved adding live entertainment to an existing bar, both in the same North Beach NCD zoning district.
The description does not state whether the business is part of a chain, so the formula retail prohibition in the North Beach NCD cannot be confirmed or ruled out.

The description states live entertainment and amplified sound but does not specify whether it is a Limited Live Performance (ending by 10 or 11 p.m., performance area ≤200 sq ft) or a Place of Entertainment (primary use, later hours, dancing or DJs), so the nighttime entertainment control is not decided.

findings.text: Police Code § 1060 et seq. requires a Place of Entertainment permit when entertainment is a primary use (live music venue, nightclub, DJs, dancing) or shows run until 2 a.m., and a Limited Live Performance permit when live performance is secondary, ending by 10 or 11 p.m. (depending on zoning) in a performance area of 200 sq ft or less.

A 2012 CUA at 1337–39 Grant Ave approved amplified live entertainment until 1:30 a.m. in conjunction with a Place of Entertainment permit, and a 2001 agency referral at this address approved non-amplified entertainment under a 1994 CUA.
The Entertainment Commission application is sent to the Police Department, Planning, DBI, Public Health, and Fire for review, and a 30-day posted notice and public hearing follow.

expected_conditions.condition: Hours of operation limited to 6 a.m. to 2 a.m. daily, with entertainment ending by 1:30 a.m. or earlier.
expected_conditions.basis: A 2012 CUA at 1337–39 Grant Ave (44 meters away) approved entertainment until 1:30 a.m. in the same North Beach NCD zoning district. The district's principally permitted hours run 6 a.m. to 2 a.m., but entertainment conditions typically impose earlier cutoffs.

expected_conditions.condition: Noise and sound limits: amplified sound levels measured at the property line or at residential units above shall not exceed ambient by more than 5 dBA, and bass frequencies attenuated to prevent low-frequency transmission.
expected_conditions.basis: Standard condition for bars and entertainment venues in mixed-use buildings in San Francisco; comparable entertainment approvals in North Beach have been conditioned on soundproofing and decibel limits, though specific limits are not extracted from the records at hand.

expected_conditions.condition: Good-neighbor policy: operator shall provide a telephone number and email address for neighbors to report concerns, respond to complaints within 24 hours, and meet quarterly with the North Beach Neighborhood Association or nearby residents.
expected_conditions.basis: Standard condition for bar and entertainment CUAs in dense residential neighborhoods; the 2012 CUA at 1337–39 Grant Ave and the 2009 CUA at 460 Columbus Ave both involved entertainment in North Beach, and good-neighbor policies are typical for such approvals citywide.

expected_conditions.condition: Security plan: operator shall submit a security plan to the Police Department and the Entertainment Commission detailing staffing, ID checks, crowd control, and procedures to prevent loitering and noise outside the premises.
expected_conditions.basis: The Entertainment Commission and Police Department review Place of Entertainment permits with an eye to public safety; security plans are routinely required for bars with entertainment in high-density areas like North Beach.

expected_conditions.condition: No physical expansion or enlargement of the bar use into adjacent spaces or floors without a new Conditional Use Authorization.
expected_conditions.basis: Planning Code § 780.3(c)(1)(A) permits intensification of an existing bar in the North Beach Special Use District only if the space is not enlarged; the 2017 CUA application to expand a bar at 1345 Grant Ave (same block) was withdrawn, suggesting expansion is more scrutinized than intensification alone.

expected_conditions.condition: Compliance with ABC Type 48 license conditions: the bar shall operate as a bona fide public premises with no minors allowed, and alcohol service shall end by 2 a.m. as required by state law.
expected_conditions.basis: ABC Type 48 is an on-sale general, public premises license that prohibits minors and is subject to standard ABC operating conditions. The license at this address was issued January 2024 and is active.

filing_playbook.action: Form the legal entity (LLC or corporation) with the California Secretary of State and obtain an EIN from the IRS.
filing_playbook.what_to_say: File Articles of Organization (LLC-1, $70) or Articles of Incorporation (ARTS-GS, $100) online at bizfile.sos.ca.gov, then apply for an EIN at irs.gov the same week. The entity name and EIN are needed for every permit, license, bank account, and lease signature that follows. If you are a sole proprietor, you may skip the entity formation and file a fictitious business name (DBA) statement with the San Francisco County Clerk instead, but an LLC or corporation is standard for a bar with a liquor license and limits personal liability.

filing_playbook.action: Register the business with the San Francisco Office of the Treasurer & Tax Collector to obtain a Business Account Number (BAN).
filing_playbook.what_to_say: Apply online at businessportal.sfgov.org within 30 days of starting business in San Francisco. The fee is tiered by gross receipts ($55 up to $100k, $95 up to $250k, $625 at $1–1.5M for 2026–27, each plus a $4 state fee). Every other city department asks for your BAN, so do this immediately after forming the entity and getting the EIN. The registration year runs April 1 to March 31 and renewal is due by the last day of February each year.

filing_playbook.action: Confirm in writing with San Francisco Planning whether intensification of entertainment and hours without physical expansion requires a new Conditional Use Authorization or can proceed under the 1994 CUA.
filing_playbook.what_to_say: Email the Planning Information Center (pic@sfgov.org) or schedule a pre-application meeting with a planner assigned to the North Beach area. Explain that 1326 Grant Ave is an existing bar with a 1994 CUA (Motion 13769) for non-amplified live entertainment, and you propose to add amplified sound and extend entertainment hours past midnight without enlarging the space. Ask: (1) Does Planning Code § 780.3(c)(1)(A) permit this as intensification without a new CUA, or does § 178 require a new CUA because a conditional use is being significantly altered? (2) If a new CUA is required, can it be processed as an amendment to Motion 13769 or must it be a new case? Request a written response or a Property Information Map report and Letter of Determination. Do not file the CUA application, the Entertainment Commission permit, or any ABC action until you have Planning's written answer, because if Pl…

filing_playbook.action: If Planning confirms a new CUA is required, file the Conditional Use Authorization application with San Francisco Planning, requesting approval to intensify entertainment by adding amplified sound and extending hours.
filing_playbook.what_to_say: Submit the CUA application online at sf.gov/departments/planning with the required fee (no-construction CUA starts at approximately $3,150 for 2026–27, CPI-adjusted annually; fees rise with construction cost). The application must include: a project description stating that this is intensification of an existing bar without physical expansion, the proposed entertainment format (Place of Entertainment or Limited Live Performance) with hours, occupant load, and floor plan, a good-neighbor plan detailing how you will address noise and security concerns, and a letter from the landlord or a copy of the lease. Planning will route the application for environmental review, schedule a pre-application community meeting (required for CUAs in neighborhood commercial districts), post a 300-foot mailed notice and a site notice for 30 days, and schedule a Planning Commission hearing. At the hearing, f…

filing_playbook.action: After the CUA is approved and the 30-day appeal period expires (or if Planning confirms no CUA is needed), apply for the Place of Entertainment or Limited Live Performance permit from the San Francisco Entertainment Commission.
filing_playbook.what_to_say: Email the Entertainment Commission Deputy Director (contact via sfgov.org/entertainment) to confirm zoning eligibility before applying; attach the approved CUA (or Planning's letter stating no CUA is needed) and a copy of the lease or ABC license. If eligible, file the application online with the $2,708 application fee (2026–27). The application must include: the CUA approval or Letter of Determination, the proposed hours and entertainment format, a floor plan showing the performance area (if Limited Live Performance, it must be ≤200 sq ft), a sound and security plan, proof of workers' compensation insurance, and the ABC license or a pending ABC application number. The Commission will refer the application to the Police Department, Planning, DBI, Public Health, and Fire for review, and you must post a yellow notice at the site for 30 days and conduct neighborhood outreach. filing_playbook.action: Apply for or confirm the ABC license with the California Department of Alcoholic Beverage Control.
filing_playbook.what_to_say: An active ABC Type 48 (on-sale general, public premises) license is on file at 1326 Grant Ave, issued January 17, 2024. If the license will remain with the same owner and entity and no transfer or amendment is needed, no new ABC application is required; confirm the license status at abc.ca.gov and ensure the premises registration and seller's permit match the entity. If the license must be transferred to a new owner or entity, file a person-to-person transfer application with ABC, which takes 90–180 days including escrow, a 30-day public posting at the premises, and local zoning sign-off from Planning. If a new license is needed (unlikely, as a Type 48 is already active here), note that Type 48 is a quota license and new ones are released only through ABC's annual priority drawing or purchased on the open market for $100k–$450k in San Francisco. ABC will refer the application to the San…

filing_playbook.action: Obtain the health permit to operate from the San Francisco Department of Public Health.
filing_playbook.what_to_say: Apply online at sfdph.org/dph/EH at least one month before opening, with your BAN, Location ID (LIN), and federal tax ID. The permit is issued after plan check (if the space is new or remodeled) and a final inspection. For a bar with no food preparation, the 2026–27 fee is $470 for the Permit to Operate application (includes initial inspection) and $0 annual license fee for 2026–28. A certified food safety manager is not required if you serve only beverages, but if you serve any food (even prepackaged snacks), at least one owner or employee must have a Certified Food Protection Manager certificate (ServSafe or equivalent, $100–$250) before the pre-opening inspection. Schedule the final health inspection two weeks in advance; DPH will refer the permit application to Planning for zoning review, and Planning will confirm the CUA approval.

filing_playbook.action: Obtain music licensing (ASCAP and BMI) and complete RBS training for all alcohol servers and managers.
filing_playbook.what_to_say: Federal copyright law requires a blanket public performance license to play music (background, DJs, live covers, TV with music). Apply online at ascap.com and bmi.com; annual fees are formula-based on occupancy and music use (typically $300–$2,500 per catalog). Most venues need both ASCAP and BMI because their catalogs do not overlap. California AB 1221 requires Responsible Beverage Service (RBS) certification for every alcohol server and their managers within 60 days of hire. Register on the ABC RBS Portal at abc.ca.gov/licensing/rbs ($3), complete an approved course (about $10–$25), and pass the exam. Keep the certification list on site for ABC inspections. These are fast (1–7 days each) but easy to forget, so schedule them in the final two weeks before opening.

timeline_cost.notes: The timeline and cost range cover the Conditional Use Authorization (120–300 days, $3,100–$15,000), the Place of Entertainment or Limited Live Performance permit (45–120 days, $2,708), and the health permit to operate (14–45 days, $470), which are the approvals in the entitlement path. These are times to approval for cases that are granted; denied or withdrawn cases are not included in this range. The CUA is the critical path: pre-application meeting, environmental review, community meeting, 300-foot mailed notice, 30-day posted notice, and Planning Commission hearing, followed by a 30-day appeal period, typically take six to ten months when approved. The Entertainment Commission permit follows the CUA and adds two to four months (intake meeting, referrals to five departments, 30-day posted notice, and Commission hearing). The health permit is administrative and takes two to six weeks after the CUA is approved. The cost does not include the ABC license because the description does not state whether the existing Type 48 license will be transferred, amended, or remain unchanged, so no ABC cost is included. If a Type 48 transfer is needed, add 90–180 days and $17,000–$450,000 (license purchase price plus transfer fees). The cost also does not include business registration ($55–$700), entity formation ($70–$150), a fictitious business name ($60–$120), workers' compensation insurance (premiums are a percentage of payroll, not a government fee), music licensing ($600–$5,000 for ASCAP and BMI combined), or RBS training ($13–$150 for five employees), because these are not discretionary approvals and are required for any bar. The timeline assumes no discretionary review, no neighborhood appeal to the Board of Supervisors, and no revisions required by the Entertainment Commission; protests or appeals can add three to six months.
